title: Canonical Evolution of Enterprise Open Source RISC-V at Hot Chips 2026
gist: Canonical's Hot Chips 2026 presentation shows Ubuntu on RISC-V has reached the RVA23 baseline with ~95% package parity to amd64, but test-pass rates lag badly (55.1% vs. ~92% on amd64), signaling RISC-V is architecturally standardized but still software-immature for enterprise deployment as server-class RVA23 hardware arrives from multiple vendors in 2026-2027.

insights.claim: Canonical's core design principle is that an Ubuntu system should behave identically regardless of underlying processor architecture, achieved by running every new ISA through the same package build, release, and long-term maintenance pipeline used for x86 and Arm.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: This 'uniform experience across ISAs' strategy is what determines whether RISC-V can plausibly be adopted in enterprise/datacenter settings without bespoke porting work — a key enabler (or bottleneck) for RISC-V server uptake.
insights.quote: Canonical says its work is not done until it can long-term patch and maintain the released binary aggregation and deliver a unified Ubuntu experience, meaning every new architecture has to flow through the same release and maintenance cycle.

insights.claim: Ubuntu's Main package archive (~3,000 packages) offers long-term support up to 15 years under Ubuntu Pro, while the larger Universe archive (~30,000 packages) is community-supported with a shorter window; Canonical maintains a portfolio of kernels tuned specifically for hyperscaler and silicon partners.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: The 15-year Main-archive support window under Ubuntu Pro is a concrete enterprise-procurement lever Canonical can point to when selling RISC-V-based servers into long-lifecycle enterprise/government deployments, once RISC-V packages migrate into Main.

insights.claim: Ubuntu already supports a wide range of architectures beyond x86 and Arm, including IBM POWER and IBM Z mainframes, framing RISC-V as simply the newest entrant into an established multi-ISA support model rather than a novel undertaking.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Canonical's multi-decade experience supporting niche ISAs (POWER, Z) is evidence it has the institutional process to bring RISC-V to enterprise-grade maturity, reducing execution risk relative to a from-scratch effort.
insights.quote: RISC-V may sound exotic, but Ubuntu supports not only Arm and x86 CPUs but also IBM POWER and Z mainframes.
insights.locator: section on Canonical ISA support in Ubuntu

insights.claim: Ubuntu's RISC-V (riscv64) baseline moved from the older RVA20 profile to the RVA23 profile starting with Ubuntu 25.10, a major architectural upgrade requiring vector operations, hypervisor support, and bit manipulation instructions out of the box.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: RVA23 becoming the standard baseline is a concrete milestone marking RISC-V's transition from fragmented, per-vendor extension sets to a unified enterprise application baseline — the key precondition for third-party software vendors to target RISC-V with a single build.
insights.quote: This RISC-V riscv64 target moved from the RVA20 profile to the RVA23 profile with Ubuntu 25.10.
insights.locator: section on Canonical ISA support in Ubuntu

insights.claim: RVA23 profile ratification and server platform ratification are both complete, with server-class RVA23 hardware expected from multiple vendors during 2026 and 2027.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: A concrete 2026-2027 hardware-availability window for server-class RVA23 silicon gives investors a timeline for when RISC-V-based servers could become commercially viable enterprise infrastructure options, a potential long-term competitive threat to Arm/x86 server incumbents.
insights.quote: The RVA23 profile ratification is done, and so is server platform ratification, with server-class RVA23 hardware expected from multiple vendors in 2026 and 2027.
insights.locator: section on Canonical Evolving ISA standards and profiles

insights.claim: Beyond baseline profiles, Ubuntu 25.10 introduced architecture variants that allow packages to be built multiple times targeting different CPU feature levels (e.g., an amd64v3 variant adding AVX2, FMA, and BMI2 while retaining backward compatibility) — a pattern Canonical plans to replicate for future RISC-V profiles.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Applying the amd64v3-style variant-build pattern to RISC-V would let Canonical ship performance-optimized RISC-V builds without breaking compatibility with older RISC-V silicon, mirroring how x86 has balanced backward compatibility with newer instruction sets — a scalable template for managing RISC-V's fragmented extension landscape.
insights.locator: section on Canonical ISA support in Ubuntu (architecture variants)

insights.claim: RISC-V package coverage in Ubuntu has reached about 95% parity with amd64 builds, indicating the software catalog has largely caught up in breadth.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: 95% package availability parity suggests RISC-V is no longer meaningfully behind on raw software catalog breadth, shifting the real adoption bottleneck to quality/reliability (test pass rates) rather than mere package existence.
insights.quote: Around 95% of packages are currently available on RISC-V compared with amd64
insights.locator: section on Canonical Packages status and statistics

insights.claim: On an Ubuntu 26.10 test snapshot, RISC-V posted only a 55.1% package test pass rate (1,898 of 3,443 packages tested) versus roughly 92% on amd64, with Canonical attributing the gap partly to reliance on emulated build/test targets that stretch execution from hours to days, and partly to fewer packages having tests at all on RISC-V.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: The 55.1% vs. ~92% test-pass gap is the clearest quantified evidence that RISC-V remains materially less mature than x86 for production/enterprise workloads despite near-parity package counts — a concrete metric to track quarter-over-quarter as a leading indicator of true RISC-V server readiness, separate from marketing claims of 'catching up.'
insights.quote: With 3,443 packages under test and 1,898 passing, RISC-V posts about a 55.1 percent pass rate on an Ubuntu 26.10 test snapshot, well below the roughly 92 percent seen on amd64.
insights.locator: section on Canonical Package Test Statistics Across Architectures

insights.claim: Canonical is addressing the test-execution bottleneck by adding native RISC-V build/test hardware (rather than relying solely on emulation) with help from partners supplying server-grade RVA23 platforms.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: The shift from emulated to native RISC-V build/test infrastructure is a direct causal lever for closing the test-pass-rate gap; watch for Canonical's next Hot Chips or Ubuntu release update on this specific metric as a proxy for RISC-V maturation speed.
insights.locator: section on Canonical Package Test Statistics Across Architectures

insights.claim: Snap package support on RISC-V remains a work in progress because most publicly available snaps currently target client/desktop use cases rather than server workloads; the author notes ServeTheHome's own team generally prefers apt over snaps regardless.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Snap immaturity on RISC-V is a secondary but real gap for developers relying on Canonical's newer packaging format, though the author's aside suggests it may matter less for server/enterprise use cases that predominantly use apt.
insights.quote: Snap support is still a work in progress because most publicly available snaps today target the client and desktop ecosystem.
insights.locator: section on Canonical Packages status and statistics

themes.theme: Ecosystem collaboration and production readiness roadmap

insights.claim: Canonical Kubernetes and MicroCloud are being actively ported to native RISC-V for container orchestration and edge-cloud use cases, indicating Canonical's cloud-native stack (not just base OS) is being extended to RISC-V.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Porting Kubernetes/MicroCloud to RISC-V signals Canonical is targeting real cloud/edge deployment scenarios for RISC-V, not just base-OS compatibility, which is necessary (though not sufficient) for datacenter operators to consider RISC-V servers viable.
insights.locator: section on Canonical Product Maturity Roadmap on RISC-V

insights.claim: Canonical participates in the RISE Project alongside RISC-V International, targeting commercial software readiness across mobile, consumer electronics, datacenter, and automotive markets, with a build/board farm hosted at Scaleway Elastic Metal using Alibaba and SpacemiT hardware that has run 24,000 jobs and 700,000 minutes of native RISC-V builds across 116 organizations.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: The scale of the RISE build farm (24,000 jobs, 116 organizations) is a concrete measure of ecosystem breadth and cross-vendor investment (Alibaba, SpacemiT) behind RISC-V software readiness, useful for gauging how broad-based (vs. single-vendor-dependent) the RISC-V push currently is.
insights.locator: section on Canonical Open source collaboration

insights.claim: The author concludes that with server-class RVA23 hardware arriving over the next two years, the RISC-V software stack finally has a fixed target to converge on, but explicitly cautions that there is still considerable ground to cover before RISC-V becomes mainstream.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: A balanced, non-hyped closing assessment (fixed target now exists, but substantial maturity gap remains) is a useful calibration against more bullish RISC-V narratives — implies enterprise-grade RISC-V servers are a 2027+ story, not an imminent one.
insights.quote: With server-class RVA23 hardware arriving over the next two years, the software stack now has a fixed target to converge on. Hopefully this moves RISC-V into a more mainstream role. Still, it seems like there is quite a bit of ground to cover.
